claim: RIBEYE is the major protein associated with the ribbon.
source: RIBEYE is the major protein associated with the ribbon (Zanazzi and Matthews, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zanazzi and Matthews, 2009

claim: RIBEYE consists of a unique amino-terminal A domain, which forms the ribbon scaffold.
source: It consists of a unique amino-terminal A domain, which forms the ribbon scaffold, and a carboxy-terminal B domain with lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase activity, which is almost identical to CtBP2, a transcriptional co-repressor (Schmitz et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmitz et al., 2000

claim: RIBEYE has a carboxy-terminal B domain with lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase activity, which is almost identical to CtBP2, a transcriptional co-repressor.
source: It consists of a unique amino-terminal A domain, which forms the ribbon scaffold, and a carboxy-terminal B domain with lysophosphatidic acid acyltransferase activity, which is almost identical to CtBP2, a transcriptional co-repressor (Schmitz et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmitz et al., 2000

claim: The ribbon is anchored to the presynaptic membrane by Bassoon protein in mammalian IHCs.
source: The ribbon is anchored to the presynaptic membrane by Bassoon protein in mammalian IHCs (Khimich et al., 2005) as well as in retinal photoreceptors and bipolar cells (Dick et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Khimich et al., 2005 and Dick et al., 2001

claim: The ribbon is anchored to the presynaptic membrane by Bassoon protein in retinal photoreceptors and bipolar cells.
source: The ribbon is anchored to the presynaptic membrane by Bassoon protein in mammalian IHCs (Khimich et al., 2005) as well as in retinal photoreceptors and bipolar cells (Dick et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dick et al., 2001

claim: The ribbon is comprised predominantly of RIBEYE.
source: Although it is comprised predominantly of RIBEYE (Zenisek et al., 2004), the ribbon complex may associate with over 30 different synaptic proteins (Uthaiah and Hudspeth, 2010; Kantardzhieva et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zenisek et al., 2004

claim: The ribbon complex may associate with over 30 different synaptic proteins.
source: Although it is comprised predominantly of RIBEYE (Zenisek et al., 2004), the ribbon complex may associate with over 30 different synaptic proteins (Uthaiah and Hudspeth, 2010; Kantardzhieva et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Uthaiah and Hudspeth, 2010 and Kantardzhieva et al., 2012

claim: IHCs respond to sound with graded receptor potentials that drive rapid and precise synaptic release, encoding intensity and timing information.
source: IHCs respond to sound with graded receptor potentials that drive rapid and precise synaptic release, encoding intensity and timing information (Fuchs, 2005; Matthews and Fuchs, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fuchs, 2005 and Matthews and Fuchs, 2010

claim: The ribbon is thought to sustain continuous encoding by tethering a pool of vesicles that replenishes the local pool of docked and primed vesicles upon depletion.
source: The ribbon is thought to sustain continuous encoding by tethering a pool of vesicles that replenishes the local pool of docked and primed vesicles upon depletion.
evidence: This is a statement of existing hypothesis in the field

claim: Postsynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at ribbon synapses range in amplitude by up to 20-fold.
source: Postsynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) at ribbon synapses range in amplitude by up to 20-fold.
evidence: This is a statement of known characteristics of EPSCs at ribbon synapses

claim: Anti-CtBP2 labelled the ribbons in wildtype (WT) but not in the KO animals (postnatal day 21, P21).
source: Anti-CtBP2 labelled the ribbons in wildtype (WT) but not in the KO animals (postnatal day 21, P21)(Figure 1A).

claim: Nuclear CtBP2 was still observed in both WT and KO.
source: Nuclear CtBP2 was still observed in both WT and KO (not shown) because the KO is specific to the RIBEYE A-domain.

claim: Bassoon and Homer puncta were similar in number in WT and KO mice.
source: Bassoon and Homer puncta were similar in number in WT and KO mice (Bassoon — 40 ± 15 in WT, 43 ± 12 in KO, p=0.76; Homer — 17 ± 3 for both WT and KO; WT — n = 20 mice, KO — n = 19 mice, p=0.64).

claim: The number of paired Homer and Bassoon puncta were similarly comparable: 14 ± 2 (n = 20) for WT and 13 ± 2 (n = 19) for KO IHCs (p=0.18).
source: The number of paired Homer and Bassoon puncta (Figure 1D) were similarly comparable: 14 ± 2 (n = 20) for WT and 13 ± 2 (n = 19) for KO IHCs (p=0.18), suggesting that synapses were formed and maintained in comparable numbers regardless of the presence of ribbons.
evidence: Supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Synapses were formed and maintained in comparable numbers regardless of the presence of ribbons.
source: The number of paired Homer and Bassoon puncta (Figure 1D) were similarly comparable: 14 ± 2 (n = 20) for WT and 13 ± 2 (n = 19) for KO IHCs (p=0.18), suggesting that synapses were formed and maintained in comparable numbers regardless of the presence of ribbons.
evidence: Inferred from the quantitative data showing no difference in paired puncta

claim: The KO presynaptic synapses consistently showed a small osmiophilic density in contact with the pre-synaptic membrane at the center of the synapse, which resembled the arciform density seen at ribbon synapses in the retina.
source: The KO presynaptic synapses consistently showed a small osmiophilic density in contact with the pre-synaptic membrane at the center of the synapse, which resembled the arciform density seen at ribbon synapses in the retina.
evidence: Observation from TEM and tomography data

claim: We found no spatial organization of vesicles near active zones in KO IHCs, suggestive of the 'ghost' ribbons observed in the zebrafish lateral-line hair cells.
source: We found no spatial organization of vesicles near active zones in KO IHCs, suggestive of the 'ghost' ribbons observed in the zebrafish lateral-line hair cells (Lv et al., 2016).

claim: In the KO mouse, IHCs lack synaptic ribbons and have no obvious compensatory structures.
source: Thus, in the KO mouse, IHCs lack synaptic ribbons and have no obvious compensatory structures.

claim: In the WT, the average vesicle diameter was 33.6 ± 3 nm (n = 21), and in the KO, it was 33.8 ± 3 nm (n = 21).
source: In the WT, the average vesicle diameter was 33.6 ± 3 nm (n = 21), and in the KO, it was 33.8 ± 3 nm (n = 21).

source: Total vesicle numbers were 20 ± 2 for WT and 7 ± 3 for KO, significantly greater for WT compared with KO synapses (p<0.001, Welch correction for unequal variance).

claim: DPOAE threshold measurements were not different across frequencies from 4 to 46 kHz.

claim: ABR thresholds were elevated by approximately 10 dB at all probe frequencies in KO mice.

claim: There was no difference in the number of puncta between WT and KO for CaV1.3 (20 ± 6, n = 9 vs. 18 ± 5, n = 13, p=0.51) or GluA3 (15 ± 3, n = 9 vs. 15 ± 2, n = 13, p=0.43).

claim: There was also no difference in the number of paired synaptic puncta between genotypes, with values of 14 ± 2 (n = 9) for WT and 13 ± 2 (n = 13) for KO (p=0.13).
source: There was also no difference in the number of paired synaptic puncta between genotypes, with values of 14 ± 2 (n = 9) for WT and 13 ± 2 (n = 13) for KO (p=0.13).

claim: The presence of the ribbon did not influence the number of apparently functional synapses in each IHC.
source: Thus, the presence of the ribbon did not influence the number of apparently functional synapses in each IHC.

claim: GluA3 puncta were larger on average in the KO.

source: The volumes of the CaV1.3 and Bassoon distributions were very similar among genotypes, but the volume of Bassoon was significantly higher in KO.

source: Half activation voltages were −34 ± 0.3 mV (n = 18, WT) and −33.4 ± 0.3 mV (n = 26, KO) for animals P10–P13.

claim: No evidence was found for partial or defective ribbons structures, nor did we detect compensation by other proteins in the absence of RIBEYE.

claim: No change in vesicle size or maximal release supports the conclusion that the ribbon is not involved in vesicle formation.
